extracted.intended_audience: owners/operators of electric utilities and independent power producers, state regulators, environmental counsel, and other stakeholders affected by CCR (coal combustion residuals) regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and regulatory standards for identifying which inactive CCR surface impoundments are 'legacy' units subject to the final CCR rule, how applicability is determined (date, presence of liquids, facility status), and how certain closure/documentation scenarios are treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'Legacy CCR Surface Impoundment'
rubrics_metrics.description: A legacy CCR surface impoundment must meet three criteria: (1) The unit meets the definition of a CCR surface impoundment; (2) The unit contains both CCR and liquids on or after October 19, 2015; and (3) The unit is located at an inactive electric utility or independent power producer. This definition is codified in §257.53.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three criteria must be met for an inactive impoundment to be a legacy CCR surface impoundment. EPA estimated the number of such units and codified the definition at §257.53.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability date for legacy designation
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule adopts October 19, 2015 as the date for determining applicability: an inactive impoundment that contained both CCR and liquids on or after that date is a legacy CCR surface impoundment subject to the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA chose Oct 19, 2015 because it is consistent with the USWAG decision, restores the status quo vacated by the court, and is the most protective option. EPA considered and rejected using the effective date of the final rule as an alternative applicability date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of both CCR and liquids is a trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: A unit must have contained both CCR and liquids on or after the applicability date (Oct 19, 2015) to be a legacy impoundment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explained that retaining oversight of units that may have been dewatered but not yet completed closure is important because precipitation and groundwater can generate leachate; units that still contain liquid present different risks and are therefore treated differently under the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of dewatered or closed units (risk remains)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if impoundments have been partially or fully dewatered, or have completed some form of closure, they can still present significant risks to human health and the environment due to existing or ongoing groundwater contamination and residual saturation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes that partial dewatering often leaves porewater and residual liquids; units intersecting groundwater remain saturated; past releases may persist and migrate. Thus dewatered or closed status alone does not remove the unit from concern or regulatory coverage unless specific closure-by-removal documentation is provided (see §257.102(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure-by-removal documentation exempts site from further CCR requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A facility that documents that it meets the standard for closure by removal in §257.102(c) will not be subject to any further requirements under the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA recognizes it lacks jurisdiction where closure-by-removal meets the §257.102(c) standard; facilities must document meeting that standard to be exempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Units that completed closure with waste in place before effective date — modified requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A facility that completed closure with waste in place before the effective date of the final rule will be subject only to the closure performance standards in §257.102(d) and the post-closure care requirements (groundwater monitoring and corrective action, if necessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where closure was completed under a regulatory authority's oversight (e.g., State or Federal cleanup order), such units could be subject to fewer requirements and EPA may defer assessment of adequacy to a subsequent permitting authority on a site-specific basis. In the interim these units would be subject to a post-closure care permit (groundwater monitoring and corrective action if necessary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-faith evidence standard for historical determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners and operators are expected to develop a strategy to gather readily available and reliable information to determine whether an inactive impoundment contained CCR and liquids on Oct 19, 2015. If, after making a good faith effort, a facility is genuinely unable to obtain information to document that the impoundment contained both CCR and liquids on that date, the unit would not be regulated as a legacy impoundment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA does not require acquisition of records that no longer exist; the standard is reasonable, documented, and based on a good faith effort to obtain available records and information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation of requirements by presence of liquid
rubrics_metrics.description: Units that contain liquid present different risks than those that do not, and applicable requirements should differentiate among them accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explains that units with liquids (or with conditions that sustain saturation) pose ongoing leaching and hydraulic head risks; therefore rule requirements vary depending on whether liquids are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors indicating higher risk from legacy impoundments
rubrics_metrics.description: Legacy impoundments are likely to pose greater risks because they are more likely to be unlined, more likely not to have been designed by a professional engineer, more likely to contain a mix of coal ash and coal refuse, older (average ~55 years), and in some instances structurally unstable or have hydraulic head promoting continuous leaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cites these factors (absence of liner, coal refuse mixing, age, structural instability, construction intersecting groundwater, hydraulic head) and modeling showing peak releases may not occur until ~70 years after placement to justify regulation and the applicability date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction relative to groundwater elevates risk
rubrics_metrics.description: If any portion of the unit is constructed in or below the water table, continuous saturation by groundwater allows continuous leaching into nearby ground and surface waters even without ponded hydraulic head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA contrasts diked impoundments above the water table (where dewatering reduces hydraulic head but porewater and residual liquids may remain) with units intersecting groundwater that remain a source of continuous contamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-approved closures are not automatically sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA will not accept all State closures as sufficient to avoid Federal requirements, because State programs vary in protectiveness and some closures lacked groundwater monitoring or other verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA surveyed State regulation and found a wide range of protectiveness; absence of consistent, sufficiently protective State approaches supports need for uniform Federal standards. Some units closed under State oversight may nonetheless be subject to post-closure care pending site-specific evaluation by permitting authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of heavily vegetated or redeveloped sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Sites that are heavily vegetated or redeveloped are not automatically exempted from requirements; EPA contends that potential disruption of current land use is outweighed by the need to address ongoing threats from inadequately closed units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes no commenters submitted data demonstrating that remediation or reopening would be more detrimental to health/environment than cleaning up contamination; current record does not support exemptions for such sites that still contain both liquids and CCR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retroactivity/ reliance-interest analysis for applicability date
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's use of Oct 19, 2015 as an applicability date is not impermissibly retroactive because the rule relies on a past fact to support future application of regulations, sets future compliance dates (so no penalties for pre-effective-date noncompliance), and accounts for reliance interests via compliance deadlines and deferred requirements where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA distinguishes primary retroactivity (impermissible alteration of past legal consequences) from permissible secondary effects; it cites case law (Bowen, Bergerco, USWAG) and explains why the rule survives retroactivity challenges.
